title: Join Us at RAMHT-AI This Sunday in San Fransisco.
subtitle: It's like a newsletter...LIVE!
body_html:
I'm lucky to have the friends that I have. One of those is Grady Hannah, who gave me a nudge several years back.

“Owen, we gotta do a live version of your newsletter.”

Not all ideas are obviously good at first. Maybe it was my own self-doubt, or perhaps it was seeing live-action versions of the Planet Money and Radiolab podcasts, both of which are real production numbers. I couldn't possibly live up to that!

Well, Grady Hannah was right, and I was wrong. This Sunday, we are throwing the fifth Rapid Acting Mental Health Treatment event, this time incorporating our long-standing belief that AI is part of the future, in the name of the event: RAMHT-AI. He’s now the CEO of an AI startup…

The idea, from the start, was to have an event where the talks were bite-sized, concise, and high value. There are a lot of conferences with mind-numbingly bland thought leadership, but the audience doesn't get much out of it; it's more about the person on stage.

At RAMHT-AI, we made the talks rapid fire. Each individual conversation between a diad is all of 10 minutes. When we have a panel discussion, and there are only two this year, it's only 20 minutes. If you got something good to say, say it now. Don't have it go on and on, because at the end of the day, if you say something interesting, and someone in the audience wants to talk to you about it, there should be time for that!

So that's what we do! It's been a remarkable success in a number of regards. The first thing that's really cool about it to me is that connections have been made that have led to real changes in the world. I'm gonna give you an example:

One of our speakers this year, Tanel Petelot, I actually met at a prior RAMHT. Now, there's a clinical trial in the works, and his product, Emobot, is already tracking the moods of thousands of people—passively, throughout their day!

It's also led to friendships, and in some cases, companies being founded, and in other cases, companies being funded! We heard the announcement of Sanmai’s existence publicly at the very first event, and their transcranial focused ultrasound technology is funded by Reid Hoffman, among others. The first public unveiling of our deeply missed friend Nolan Williams’ data on Ibogaine was at that very first RAMHT event as well.

I couldn't be more excited for the people joining us this year. I wanna just do a little jumping up and down for the conversations I get to have—and I hope you're going to join us to hear!

  • Jonathan Seltzer, CEO of SimplePractice, joins us for a conversation. He is the deeply gracious and very funny CEO of a software company that makes a low-cost, scalable, and very broadly used electronic health record for Therapists and Psychiatrists. Having come from a world of private equity investment, he understood that individual practitioners need tools to do their job, but don't necessarily want to spend an arm and a leg. The big boys in electronic health record technology, like EPIC, don't have independent practices as customers, and many people are selling EHR technology to practices that weren't focused on letting them stay independent, and that meant keeping overhead down. My first company, Brooklyn Minds, used this software for many years. The product may be software, but the customers are independent, and the focus on that usually interesting for me to hear. How do we give individuals market power to become entrepreneurs in their own lives?

  • Kirk Thelander, Chief Commercial Officer, GrayMatters Health: I love Kirk, as a person. That's a personal disclosure. Kirk is a lifetime member of our “directly treats the brain” as a life’s work team. At Grey Matters Health, they are bringing a system called PRISM to the world, and it's so cool. We've had Oded Kraft, their CEO, on the main stage before, but it's a treatment in which the brain stimulator is your own brain. I was introduced to EEG neurofeedback as a treatment by none other than Bessel Van Der Kolk, the most popular writer in psychiatry. PRISM takes what was a promising approach and turned it into a real technology. They have a treatment for PTSD, and an emerging treatment for anhedonia in major depressive disorder, and it's among the safest treatments I've ever encountered. The risk profile is similar to thinking hard. But, they're probably gonna have something new to tell us that even I don't know about, and I'm really excited to hear what they have next.

  • Dominik Middelmann, Co-Founder & CEO, MDHub, will be speaking with Carlene Macmillan, M.D., and they make the AI technology that has saved me thousands of hours thus far. We've all talked about the power of AI before, endlessly, but MDHub was the first product that really made my life dramatically better. I absolutely use it more than any other AI product in my clinical work. He's also pretty funny. It's not an official criterion for being a speaker, but it doesn’t hurt.

  • Jonathan Javitt, MD, MPH, Founder, Chairman, and CEO, NRx Pharmaceuticals, Inc. Jonathan and I have great taste in blazers. That's the most important thing for you to know. The first time I met him, it was at the behavioral health technology conference, and here's what we looked like:

    NRx is a pharma company, but it's also given rise to Hope Therapeutics, another healthcare services company that delivers effective treatments for mental health conditions—such as ketamine and transcranial magnetic stimulation —and, I imagine, more in the future. They made waves earlier this year, submitting an NDA for an on-label version of intravenous ketamine for depression to the FDA, and I imagine he's got more to say as well! You're gonna notice a theme here—Hope Theraputics is at least in theory “competitive” with other healthcare delivery services companies. I see it as working, in parallel, to create a movement. That theme flows throughout this meeting! There are novel treatments that are the future, and hearing from people working on that from different angles? That is what RAMHT is all about.

  • Josh Stevens, CEO at Beckley Clinical, is someone with whom I have a real bromance. Josh is an actuary by training and has a keen eye for what makes a business actually work, but he's building large-scale infrastructure to make ketamine-assisted therapy, brain stimulation, and other (future) psychedelic modalities accessible. If you're noticing that that might be “directly competitive” with what I do with my day at Radial, you're both correctish and wrong about the scale of the problem. It's like saying having more than one hospital is too many. I've heard Josh has some big news for us, but we'll have to wait and see.

  • Srinivas Rao, MD, PhD, CEO & Co-Founder of AtaiBeckley: I couldn't be more excited to have Dr. Rao join us from AtaiBeckley. After a recent merger and redomiciling in the US (which is a big deal because your stock can be part of index funds), the Atai and Beckley teams came together to bring a series of new psychedelic medicines to the world.

    Along with Compass Pathways and MindMed, and others, we have remarkable leadership at the helm of a series of companies focused on creating treatments. They're different from everything we've known before. I can't wait for Dr Rao to tell us as much as he can about what AtaiBeckley is up to now and what we have to prepare for.

  • Edwin Wong, PhD, CEO of Psyrin, is part of our remarkable team that's building AI tools to harness the power of the sound of our voices. Psyrin uses vocal biomarker technology to understand what's behind what we say. Some of that is tools to make clinical workflows easier, and the underlying technology we're running clinical trials on right now at Radial may be the next wave in psychiatric diagnostic adjuvant technology. I interviewed one of his co-founders at length here.

  • Jonathan Downar, MD, PhD, Co-Founder of Ampa Health, has become such a dear friend over the past few years. I had seen his name on papers in my field for years. This is the guy who ran the Three-D trial. And then, like so many of us, he became an entrepreneur. Also, pulling together a team around the idea that TMS should be available everywhere, for everyone. They built a TMS treatment device, now cleared by the FDA, that's light, inexpensive, and really easy to train people to use accurately. They combined TMS treatment with an ancient tuberculosis drug, d-cycloserine, because it turns out that it increases your brain's ability to change. Their pioneering research on a one-day TMS treatment, and who knows what else. Well, the people who will know what else are the people who come to RAMHT. I have my own series of papers coming out with Jonathan as a co-author, and most importantly, he's a deeply gracious person.

  • Carlene MacMillan, MD, FCTMSS, DFAACAP, Chief Product Officer & Co-Founder, Radial, is listed last, but certainly not least. She's not only a cofounder at the company at which we both work, but she's also my wife. Radial just announced the largest Series A funding round in the history of mental health technology. Dr. MacMillan is trained as a physician. She has made a career change—she's now the Chief Product Officer at Radial. She has really strong feelings about the customer experience, where that overlaps with traditional medical and patient experience ideas, and where we can draw inspiration from companies like Duolingo, Amazon, and other consumer-facing companies.

And that's just the people on the stage. Chris from Hydra strategies is behind the scenes, making sure this whole event is possible, as well as many others. If I were Gen Alpha, I would tell you that “low-key”, the real goal is to have the audience members be the most exciting part of the event. I might even add “ngl.”

Having seen who has already bought tickets, I'm pretty sure that's likely to be the case.

RAMHT-AI 2026 Happens Sunday, January 11th!

Use code “RAMHTJPM” to get your FREE ticket.

Free RAMHT Tickets with CODE

I love these folks. You might too. Get ready for a night of big announcements, new technologies, new treatment models, innovative ways to think about business, innovative ways to think about patient care, and a focus on a future where people get better quickly, excessively, and safely from the brain disorders that once ailed them.
